Thanks again for the demo earlier — Marcus and team. Useful session. A few immediate items from our side so we can scope procurement and infra: 

1) SDK + auth: we currently plan to run the Redwood SDK from our EKS control plane (internal services) and the patient-facing web tier will call our backend. Do you have a recommended auth pattern? We prefer short-lived tokens and OIDC if possible. Any sample flow or config for the SDK to rotate credentials automatically?

2) Routing and fallbacks: for critical patient-facing flows (<200ms p95 target) we'd like to route to a lower-latency region and failover to a cheaper variant if capacity constrained. Can you outline how routing policies are configured and whether we can pin model versions to routes?

3) Structured output/tool calling: We plan to use tool-calls for appointment booking (calendar API) and a structured JSON schema for clinical summaries. How does Redwood handle schema validation + function/tool calling in your hosted and dedicated modes?

4) Embeddings/reranker: we will index internal clinical docs; can you confirm embedding model options and whether the reranker is run in-line or as a separate step? Cost/throughput implications appreciated.

5) Dedicated capacity sizing: preliminary concurrency is 220 concurrent sessions at peak, average request length ~120 tokens in/out, with occasional long summaries up to 1,500 tokens. What initial GPU pool sizing and queue configurations should we plan for? Also, how do autoscale policies behave with burst capacity?

Would appreciate a short post-call note we can attach to our procurement packet. Thanks — Sam

--
Sam Fisher

Fletcher Health

Sam — great questions. Putting together a concise follow-up that you can add to procurement. Below is an initial write-up plus a couple of action items for next steps. Happy to jump on a technical call with Priya and Bob if needed.

Quick answers (summary):
- Auth/SDK: Recommend OIDC with short-lived tokens (1h) + optional workload identity for EKS. We’ll provide an SDK token refresher helper and sample helm chart.
- Routing: Policy-based routing by region + model variant; yes you can pin model versions and set fallback variants (auto-fallback to quantized L-variant).
- Structured output/tool calling: Both hosted and dedicated support function calls. Dedicated lets you run schema validation inside the runtime (optional) and attach a pre/post-processing hook for validation.
- Embeddings/rerank: We support offline embedding generation or inline embedding calls. Reranking can be positioned as a separate async stage to reduce critical-path latency.
- Dedicated sizing: For 220 concurrent sessions with typical 120-token exchanges, estimate initial pool of 4x A100-equivalent GPUs (or 8x for conservative headroom) with queue-based concurrency control. Autoscale can add burst nodes within 2–5 minutes.

Attachments: redwood-dedicated-sizing-v1.xlsx (initial estimate), architecture diagram for a recommended control-plane arrangement.

Action items:
1) Monica to share the detailed sizing workbook and cost delta for inline vs async reranker.
2) Irene to send sample SDK helm chart + OIDC config.
3) Marcus to schedule a 45-min technical deep-dive (suggest Wed 8/4 morning PT).

If that works, we'll include a one-page summary formatted for procurement.

Thanks,
Marcus

Sam / Priya / Bob — sharing the detailed sizing workbook (attached) and a short compare table below to help procurement:

- Inline reranker: single request path, higher p95 latency, simpler consistency guarantees. Good for <100ms p95 slack.
- Async reranker: separate job (nearline), lower impact on p95, better cost at scale for high concurrency.

Sizing assumptions used in workbook: 220 concurrent sessions, 120 tokens typical, 2.5 requests per session average, 30% recency vector length for embeddings. Workbook shows both conservative (8x A100 equivalent) and efficient (4x + smart caching + batching) configurations.

Attachment stub: redwood-dedicated-sizing-v1.xlsx (spreadsheet with node counts, qps per device, estimated monthly cost)

Next steps: please review the workbook and tell us whether you prefer latency-first (inline) or cost-first (async) reranking. We'll prepare a final procurement-friendly summary.

Hi all — adding the technical config snippets below (quick reference). I can put these into a repo if you'd like.

1) SDK + OIDC (EKS):
- Use workload identity to mint short-lived tokens for service accounts. The SDK will refresh tokens every 45 minutes by default. Example env vars: REDWOOD_OIDC_ISSUER, REDWOOD_CLIENT_ID, REDWOOD_AUDIENCE.
- Helm values: redwood.sdk.enabled=true, redwood.auth.mode=oidc, redwood.auth.token_lifetime=3600

2) Routing + pinning:
- Routing policy YAML: routeSelector: region:us-west-2; modelPin: gpt-rl-1.2.0; fallback: gpt-rl-1.1.0-quant
- Fallbacks can be tiered: region fallback -> variant fallback -> capacity-fallback which routes to a cheaper pool with higher batch sizes.

3) Structured output/tool-calls:
- Dedicated mode supports in-runtime function call hooks. Define functions in the prompt manifest, validate with JSON schema on the runtime. Optionally, set validateOnGenerate: true to reject invalid outputs.

4) Embeddings & rerank:
- Embed offline for search index: run batched embedding jobs (we recommend 2048 token chunks).
- Rerank patterns: either inline (same request, additional embed call + kNN) or async (generate candidate set, then background rerank). Async reduces p95 by keeping heavy compute out of the critical path.

5) Autoscale & queues:
- Autoscale policy: minPool=2, targetUtil=70%, maxPool=12, scaleUpCooldown=120s. Burst capacity: add warm nodes up to +50% within 2–5 minutes.
- Concurrency control: global request queue with per-customer concurrency caps. We recommend initial per-customer concurrency cap of 300 and per-GPU concurrency 8 (adjustable).

If you want, I'll drop these snippets into a small repo and include a sample deployment manifest.

Cheers,
Irene
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
